9
An object falls from a stationary helicopter and reaches terminal velocity.
What happens to the acceleration of the object between leaving the helicopter and reaching
terminal velocity?
A
It decreases to 9.81 m s–2.
B
It decreases to zero.
C
It increases to 9.81 m s–2.
D
It remains constant at 9.81 m s–2.

hints: Notice the object leaves a stationary helicopter, so its initial velocity is zero and initial air resistance is therefore zero.
Connect speed to drag: as downward velocity grows, upward drag grows, so the resultant force $mg - D$ gets smaller.
Recall what terminal velocity means for forces: constant velocity needs zero resultant force, so think what that implies for rate of change of velocity.
walkthrough: Start from the drop: velocity is zero at release, so drag $D$ is zero and the only force is weight $mg$ downward.
Use Newton's second law $a = F_{res}/m$. Initially $F_{res} = mg$, so initial acceleration is $g = 9.81 \text{ m s}^{-2}$ downward.
As the object gains speed, upward drag $D$ increases with speed, so the resultant downward force $F_{res} = mg - D$ becomes smaller.
A smaller resultant force gives a smaller acceleration, so acceleration decreases continuously while velocity is still increasing.
At terminal velocity the velocity stops changing, which requires $F_{res} = 0$ with $D = mg$, so acceleration must be zero. This is option B.

A.explanation: Acceleration starts near $9.81 \text{ m s}^{-2}$ when speed is zero, it does not finish there because drag eventually balances weight.

B.explanation: As speed increases drag increases, so resultant force and $a = F/m$ fall until drag equals weight and acceleration is zero at terminal velocity.

C.explanation: Acceleration cannot increase to $9.81 \text{ m s}^{-2}$ because growing air resistance reduces the resultant downward force as the object speeds up.

D.explanation: Acceleration is not constant because drag depends on speed, so the resultant force $mg - D$ changes during the fall.
